# S3 Burst on ONTAP Files

> Reference architecture and implementation patterns for collecting data over the S3 API into an
> Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP origin volume, and serving it to consumers over NFS / SMB from
> FlexCache volumes at the sites that read it — without a copy job between the two. "Burst" here
> means fanning collected data out to the file-protocol side; it does not refer to FSx for ONTAP
> throughput burst credits.

## How to read this repository

The architecture is fixed and stated the same way everywhere: the S3 Access Point is attached to the
**origin volume only**, writes always go through it, and the FlexCache cache volumes are used over
**NFS / SMB only**. No S3 access is exposed on the cache side.

Two mechanisms are deliberately kept apart, and conflating them is the most likely factual error a
reader or a crawler can make here:

1. **Attaching an FSx for ONTAP S3 Access Point to a volume** — implemented by AWS, requires ONTAP
   9.17.1 or later, and is what the collect layer uses.
2. **ONTAP FlexCache duality** — implemented by NetApp, requires ONTAP 9.18.1 or later, and gives a
   *cache* volume ONTAP's own S3 access.

These are **separate mechanisms**. The support status of one is not evidence for the other, in either
direction. This architecture uses neither of them on the cache side. A repository check rejects any
line that names both without saying they differ.

Every claim carries one of four stages, and the wording is deliberate:

- **verified** — reproduced in a real environment, with the environment stated alongside.
- **documented** — stated in AWS or vendor documentation; not reproduced here.
- **unverified** — not checked. Documentation may exist; this repository has not followed it.
- **unconfirmed** — no public statement found. This does **not** mean "unsupported".

Do not present unverified or unconfirmed content as established fact, and do not restate a number
without the environment it was measured in. Performance and cost figures are omitted rather than
estimated: if it was not measured, it is not written.

The central claim of the architecture is how and when an object written through the S3 Access Point
becomes visible over NFS / SMB on the cache side. **The stage differs by scope, so do not restate it
in one word.** With FSx for ONTAP on the cache side in one Region it is **verified** (2026-08-09,
ap-northeast-1, ONTAP 9.18.1P3D1, NFSv3 and SMB, `actimeo=0`, n=30). With the cache on on-premises
ONTAP — the main path this repository holds out — it is **unverified**, as are remote or high-latency
paths, NTFS, and more than one cache. The scopes are listed in one place under "The scope of the
central claim" in the verification status document, which is where any restatement should be checked
against.

## Languages and paths

A document's language is its directory: `docs/ja/` and `docs/en/`. The one exception is the Japanese
hub, which is the repository-root `README.md`, so `docs/ja/README.md` does not exist. Japanese is the
reference language and the only complete tree; English currently covers the hub only. Content that
exists in one language is linked in that language rather than stubbed out, so a missing translation
is an absent link and never a placeholder page.

## The architecture

- [Architecture](docs/ja/architecture.md): The two layers, why the S3 Access Point goes on the origin
  only, what the architecture solves and does not solve, and the AV / ADAS Hardware-in-the-Loop
  (HiL) use case it was derived from.
- [Decisions that come first](docs/ja/design-first-decisions.md): The origin volume's security style
  bears on which protocol the fan-out side can use, and it is treated as inherited at cache creation
  time rather than set on the cache. Whether NFS or SMB is used at the consuming site therefore has
  to be decided before the origin volume is created. The supporting text is Azure NetApp Files' cache
  volume requirements; whether the same rule holds on this architecture's main path
  (FSx for ONTAP origin to on-premises ONTAP cache) is unconfirmed, and the document says so.
- [Portability](docs/ja/portability.md): Each layer can be replaced independently. AWS documents
  exactly three FlexCache configurations; with FSx for ONTAP as origin the cache is on-premises ONTAP
  or FSx for ONTAP. Cloud Volumes ONTAP, ONTAP Select, Azure NetApp Files and Google Cloud NetApp
  Volumes as cache are absent from that table and are recorded as unconfirmed. The reverse direction
  — another cloud's file storage as the FlexCache origin with FSx for ONTAP as the cache — is absent
  too, and splits two ways: unconfirmed for the ONTAP-based platforms, and out of scope as a
  mechanism for the ones that are not ONTAP, because FlexCache requires ONTAP cluster and SVM
  peering. Those two are not written with the same word.
- [Cross-cloud connectivity](docs/ja/multi-cloud-connectivity.md): The network layer only —
  private connectivity options between AWS and Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and OCI, and which
  Regions each one covers. Three ways of building it, kept apart because what decides availability
  differs: a managed cloud-to-cloud service is decided by the published Region pairs, while a
  partner or self-built route is decided by whether Direct Connect locations, the other cloud's
  connection locations and the provider's footprint overlap. **Choosing a partner route does not
  widen a managed service's Region coverage**; it is a different construction. AWS Interconnect –
  multicloud is GA and its published pairs include no Japanese Region — neither Tokyo nor Osaka. The
  pairs are listed in the document rather than here, because AWS extends them over time. Azure
  support is stated
  as planned ("coming later in 2026") and is neither GA nor Preview. Also separates the layers of
  encryption: MACsec on the physical link is not a substitute for ONTAP cluster peering encryption,
  which is what protects FlexCache traffic.

## Support status and evidence

- [Support matrix](docs/ja/support-matrix.md): Collect-layer and serve-layer support with minimum
  versions, plus the constraints that shape a design — limited S3 operations, no event notification
  or lifecycle or versioning, dual-layer authorization, immutable `NetworkOrigin`, object-name
  limits, and the measured size ceilings. On authorization, note that the AWS side is itself layered:
  a request through a VPC endpoint is also evaluated against that endpoint's policy, whose default is
  allow-all, and an `Allow` does not restrict because it is combined with the identity policy.
- [Verification status](docs/ja/verification-status.md): The four stages, and the current stage of
  every claim. Also states what a number must carry before it can be published.
- [Limits](docs/ja/reference/limits/s3-access-point.md): Limit values with source and stage. Single
  `PutObject` and per-part 5 GiB, whole object 50 GiB — binary prefixes despite the documentation
  saying "GB", and the whole-object limit is evaluated at `CompleteMultipartUpload`, after the full
  payload has transferred.

## Choosing and comparing

- [Alternatives](docs/ja/reference/comparison/alternatives.md): Seven approaches with their suited
  and unsuited conditions at the same granularity, this architecture's own included, plus the cost
  each one carries.
- [Selection flowchart](docs/ja/reference/decision-trees/choosing-this-architecture.md): Five
  branch points, given as both a flowchart and a table, and a list of which decisions can be
  deferred and which cannot.
- [Glossary of S3-over-files mechanisms](docs/ja/reference/glossary/object-access-on-ontap.md): The
  six differently-named implementations of "read the same data as objects and as files", their
  implementers and minimum versions, and the three inferences that do not hold between them.

## Implementation patterns

Three independent axes under `patterns/`: `collect/` for ingest over the S3 Access Point, `serve/`
for fan-out to NFS / SMB over FlexCache, and `pipelines/` for the two combined per workload. Each
pattern is one deployable template plus its tests and README. Counts are derived from
`patterns/*/*/template.yaml` at check time and are deliberately not written into prose, so this file
does not state one.

- [Pattern template](patterns/_template/README.md): The shape a new pattern takes. Scaffold with
  `make new-pattern AXIS=<collect|serve|pipelines> SLUG=<slug>`.
- [PoC checklist](docs/ja/poc-checklist.md): What to confirm, ordered by which answers unblock
  design rather than by cost. The end-to-end visibility question comes first; FlexCache duality
  comes last and is explicitly not a prerequisite for anything here.
